enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #7: Komaro's Challenge
"A perfect follow-up to the last episode—outrageous, raunchy, scary... and yet so heartwarming. I laughed my ass off, and by the end, I was in tears."

[Man, that was absolutely fantastic. Not a single complaint. The way this episode picked up from the previous one—Komaro's relationship with the teacher, her connection with Ume, and that post-credits scene—was nothing short of perfect.

It all started with Komaro wanting to offer students affordable rice balls after reading a suggestion submitted to the student council's suggestion box, and I loved how everyone on the council rallied around her. Then came the student council president's completely unhinged mother, the misunderstanding deliberately orchestrated by Arisu that somehow turned Komaro into her granddaughter, and the hilarious progression to the name "Three Generations." And throughout the entire episode, there was an endless barrage of things the characters said and did that were so wildly inappropriate they crossed just about every line imaginable.

Then there was the confrontation with the office clerk, which reminded me all over again just how terrifyingly formidable—and reassuringly dependable—Arisu can be. The way she treated Yoshino Saegusa afterward was hilarious, too. And as if all that weren't enough, the episode wrapped up with an absolutely glorious punchline involving the three delightfully naughty girls from the light music club, right before the ending theme.

And yet! Somehow, this was such a genuinely wonderful, heartwarming story that I found myself laughing through my tears. What struck me was how perfectly it embodied what I feel is at the heart of this series: the idea that you can throw all kinds of outrageous sexual humor and dirty jokes into the mix, laugh your head off, and blow everything out of proportion without ever compromising the essence of the story or the message it's trying to convey. The raunchiness doesn't undermine any of that. If anything, this episode showed just how beautifully the two can coexist.

And boy, did they go absolutely wild with it. I loved every second.

But seriously, I really did cry. It was such a beautiful story. And I laughed so damn hard, too...

I sincerely hope that works like this—and the people who create them—never disappear from the face of the Earth.]

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #6 (Total Ep. #19): Don't Cry, Baby
"A surprisingly touching episode that more than makes up for all the question marks it raises—though I imagine plenty of people won't see it that way."

[Okay, okay, I'll admit there were definitely moments that made me go, "Seriously? You've gotta be kidding me."

The father gets shot in the stomach, and somehow survives a wound like that? And we're supposed to believe Sara could take on that many members of a criminal organization all by herself, armed with nothing but a handgun and carrying a baby, while also trying to protect the father to some extent? Come on, that's just not happening. And conveniently, none of the enemies ever seem to shoot back or even charge at her. Then there's that whole sequence where she somehow gets them to shoot a stuffed animal to get out of a tight spot. It was entertaining to watch, sure, but I honestly couldn't make much sense of the action.

But you know what? None of that really matters.

What mattered was Sara and the baby, and the bond that developed from their encounter. The reason all three of them survived—though it was also part of what landed them in danger in the first place—was the genuine bond between the father and his child. It meant they had baby supplies they could put to use, and the baby was surprisingly calm about being held even in such a terrifying situation.

And as Sara continued taking care of the baby afterward, I'm sure something meaningful began to change inside her, too.

The baby, meanwhile, had been watching and listening to everything. Everyone kept calling out "Sara-san, Sara-san" whenever something came up, so the baby naturally picked up "Sara-shan."

That's why, when the father finally recovered and came to the hotel to ask Sara to place the baby in an institution—because he believed he shouldn't be involved in his child's life anymore—I think everything she'd experienced led her to say what she did.

She'd only had a tiny taste of raising a child, but it had already taught her firsthand just how difficult it could be. And what she'd come to realize was this: wasn't it precisely because of the bond he'd built with his child through caring for the baby that they were all standing there together now?

Without everything she'd gone through this time, Sara might well have simply agreed to his request.

It's hard to put into words, but this episode had something special that more than compensated for all those "Oh, come on, seriously?" moments. In a way, it was the kind of episode that reminded me of what makes anime anime.

It actually got me a little choked up.

Not that that's necessarily why I'm giving it a 9, though.]

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #7 (Total Ep. #21): Misunderstandings
"A lack of understanding of others begins with a lack of understanding of ourselves. Perhaps it's through the friction and discord that follow that this lack of understanding can eventually give way to a deeper understanding of ourselves and others—and of how things ought to be."

[This was honestly a tough episode to watch. This series has never really been one of those shows that makes me go, "Man, that was fun!" every week, but lately it's been digging deeper and deeper into people's inner turmoil—years of accumulated emotional baggage, the darkness that's been lurking inside them all along, and how they perceive and deal with those parts of themselves. Throw in all the psychological friction and interpersonal drama, and it's been one big "God, what a pain in the ass" experience. And this episode felt like the culmination of all that.

The exchanges between Momoka and Koyun in the first half were particularly excruciating. But the thing is, when something gets this uncomfortable, it's usually because it's hitting a nerve or reflecting something about myself that I'd rather not confront. So I just had to grit my teeth and keep watching.

Then came Momoka's interactions with Minato. Seriously, this girl acts like the entire world revolves around her, and yet she's this sensitive? Just how self-centered can you get? Yeah, more exhausting drama.

And then we got to Minato's part. He'd always thought he'd been managing just fine, but in reality, things had been out of alignment all along, gradually becoming twisted and distorted as he kept bottling everything up. Just as he finally reached his breaking point, an unexpected reunion with his older brother—who had matured emotionally in the meantime—came at exactly the right moment, helping Minato recognize something about himself that even he hadn't understood.

Ahh... that's me.

As someone who's very much the Minato type myself, that one really hurt, too.

There's the mutual lack of understanding between people who simply can't understand one another, the failure to understand oneself, and then another layer of misunderstanding: the failure to recognize that, however different their ways of being or behaving may be, everyone is ultimately doing what they do for their own sake.

I suppose it's through their relationships with others, and the friction those relationships create, that they'll gradually come to understand all of this.

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #5ː A Fickle Starting Line
"Is the Chiramune of its less-than-stellar (and mentally exhausting) days making a comeback? Overly poetic, excessively harem-like, and narcissistic."

[It wasn't bad... It really wasn't. But I felt like quite a bit of the "not-so-good Chiramune" we saw during the first cour had returned.

Basically, there's all that irritatingly pretentious, poetic dialogue, the endless parade of beautiful girls falling head over heels for Saku Chitose as he bounces from one to another, his equally irritating reactions to everything they say, and those moments when he gets all fired up and overly dramatic... You get the idea.

Cleaning the school pool alone with a girl? Yeah, right. What kind of school allows that? And what kind of teachers?

Then he goes on a date with another girl, only to run into a couple, including yet another girl who just has to butt in with her unsolicited comments.

I mean... come on.

I realize all of this is probably part of the groundwork the series is laying for future developments, and I certainly hope it pays off well. But when it gets this excessive, it really does become exhausting to sit through.]

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #6: ：Sometimes, Misaki Has to Try Her Best Alone!
"Given the fishing port and tuna setting, it's only fitting that this episode has its share of *ara* (rough edges)—but it's far from just a bunch of scraps. A genuinely likable episode, though seriously, do some research beforehand!"

[There's honestly not much more to say beyond what I've already written in the review headline.

As usual, including the post-credits scene, this was an episode that left me with a good feeling and a positive impression overall. That said, Misaki's sheer incompetence was so over the top that I can't deny finding her pretty irritating at times.

In this day and age, with smartphones everywhere, I could practically hear myself screaming, "Google it! Look it up! Do some research before you go! Why the hell are you just winging everything? You're taking this way too lightly! For fuck's sake!"

But then again, maybe it's precisely because she doesn't bother doing much of that that she ends up making mistakes and running into all sorts of unexpected situations. And perhaps part of the appeal is seeing how someone as hopelessly naive, scatterbrained, and stuck in her own little happy-go-lucky world as Misaki fits into this story—and whether she actually grows as a person or stays exactly the way she is.

I was also a little happy to see some familiar places, including Misakiguchi, getting the spotlight this time. Not that it affected my score, of course. (At least, I don't think it did.)

The ending felt pretty rushed, though, as if they couldn't quite fit everything in and just had to cut things off rather abruptly. Well, I guess that's part of its charm.

And then there was that utterly ridiculous game of *shiritori*. What the heck was that supposed to be?

Oh, and that boat... What was the deal with it? Did they just want to show it off? Does pressing a button summon an unmanned boat to come pick you up? I honestly couldn't figure that one out.

Anyway, all this has really made me crave some tuna...]

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #6: Visiting the Zoo
"It brought back memories of Woodbury and the Governor from *The Walking Dead*, but the sheer awfulness of it all left me thinking... What the hell was that?! Forget a different kind of zombie—this was completely off the mark!"

[After giving this series fairly high scores over the past few episodes, it's disappointing to see it fall right back into the stupidity of its early days.

And it all comes down to one thing: Aki. She's the problem. The one character who's ruining everything.

I'd thought she'd learned something and grown through her interactions with all those different people and her experiences living together with others at the mall—or wherever that was. But apparently, she hasn't grown even 0.1 millimeters.

And even that complete lack of growth feels unnatural. There was something about Aki's utterly deranged behavior and attitude this time that felt deliberately contrived, as though the writers were forcing her to act this way for the sake of the plot.

Or maybe it's just a stupid show after all.

This episode suddenly introduced us to the area around Ueno Zoo and its leader, Takamo, in a setup that immediately reminded me of Woodbury and the Governor from *The Walking Dead*.

But good grief, Aki was unbearable.

She's still going around endlessly declaring, "I'm looking for my father, who might have turned into a zombie, and if he has, I'll kill him," as though that barely comprehensible reasoning were some kind of all-purpose trump card she could pull out whenever she wanted.

And then there's Takamo, who, apparently driven out of her mind by Aki's influence, decides to accompany this completely unpredictable stranger she's only just met into a sealed-off subway station. A station where zombies supposedly shouldn't be able to get in, yet there are holes in the barriers and they already know zombies have been coming through regularly.

Seriously, what was she thinking?

And of course, despite being explicitly told not to make any noise, Aki immediately drops the flashlight she snatched from Takamo. Naturally.

Then thousands—tens of thousands, perhaps?—of zombies come flooding toward them all at once, threatening to destroy the entire base they've spent so much time building and bring everything crashing down.

And practically all of it is Aki and Takamo's fault.

Though, come to think of it, the whole premise was ridiculous to begin with. We're supposed to believe that an ordinary young woman managed to build a ranch from scratch in just two years, along with an entire system where people can apparently order hamburgers as casually as if normal food distribution were still functioning?

Come on...

Man, this episode was awful.

At this point, forget *Zombie違い*—this whole thing is *お門違い*. Completely off the mark.]
enjoymentRanking.comment_jp:

"The Walking Deadのウッドベリー、ガバナーを思い起こすもあまりの酷さに…何じゃこりゃ!ゾンビ違いならぬお門違い"
『折角ここ数話の間高評価してきたのに結局は初期のしょうもなさに戻ってしまった。それもこれもとにかくひとえにアキの存在に尽きる。こいつだけが何しろガン。いろんな人達との関わりや、モール?での共同生活などから学び成長したかと思いきや0.1ミリもしてなかった。でもその成長のなさも不自然で、今回のアキの土地狂った行動?態度?には制作サイドの?プロット上の意図的なものを感じる違和感があった。いや、ただただしょうもない作品なだけかも。今回の話は唐突に"The Walking Dead"のウッドベリーとガバナーを彷彿とさせる上野動物園周辺とそこのリーダータカモとの出会いだったが、まぁとにかくアキが酷い。今だにひたすら「ゾンビになっているかも知れない父親を探していて、もしゾンビになってたら私が殺す」というよく意味のわからない理屈をワイルドカードのようにのたまう。そしてそんな理由のわからないさっきであったばかりの連中と、封鎖してゾンビが出てくるはずがないのに穴も空いててコンスタントに出てきていることが分かっている地下鉄の駅に入っていくという、アキにあてられ急に正気を失ったとしか思えないタカモ…。そして音を出すなと言うのにお約束で他かもから奪った懐中電灯を即落とすアキ。そこには何千何万?という数のゾンビが居て一気に押し寄せてきて、これ迄築き上げてきた基地も崩壊全ておじゃん?みたいな状況に…。それもこれもほぼアキとタカモの落ち度。まぁそもそも、ただの女子がたった2年でゼロから牧場も作り、普通に流通してそうなハンバーガーまで注文出来るようなシステムを作っている時点でオカシイのだけど・・・。いやいや今回は酷かった。もう、"ゾンビ違い"は』"お門違い"ですよ。ー4点・復活

Rising from the ashes, a fallen noblewoman stands to save humanity!

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #7: Musical Chairs
"A fairly formulaic but well-executed, Western-style coming-of-age ensemble drama about an appealing female protagonist's growth, built around a clear-cut good-versus-evil narrative."

[This episode really made me feel like Japanese anime is becoming increasingly Americanized. There's the exaggerated, clear-cut good-versus-evil presentation, along with the familiar setup of a beautiful, highly capable but somewhat socially awkward female protagonist who's often perceived as "cold," "humorless," or "pragmatic to a fault." She struggles with how others see her while gradually forming bonds with her companions and finding her way forward—a very Western-style coming-of-age ensemble drama.

I also noticed a structure reminiscent of *Frieren: Beyond Journey's End*, with flashbacks to the past juxtaposed against the protagonist's present self.

Another distinctly American touch is how the show uses its presentation—scene transitions, shifts in perspective, and dramatic staging—to soften the impact of contrived or forced developments while simultaneously turning those very techniques into effective ways of highlighting the protagonist's appeal. You see this sort of thing all the time in American movies and TV dramas, and this series makes extensive use of it.

In other words, this was an episode that left me thinking, perhaps inevitably, about how the anime entertainment industry itself is becoming increasingly Americanized.

That said, the execution still isn't quite there. There are plenty of convenient plot developments and forced moments, and the storytelling often feels overly broad and sketchy, as though it's simply throwing key dramatic moments at us while skipping the steps needed to connect them.

The result is an undeniable patchwork quality—rough, loosely assembled, and lacking the necessary buildup. Important moments are suddenly presented without sufficient groundwork, making it difficult to empathize with the characters or become emotionally invested in them.

I was also disappointed by the occasional cold, bitter, almost grimacing expressions Romelia displays. Rather than feeling like natural manifestations of the personality the story has gradually established, they come across more as devices employed for dramatic effect.

Still, the series has clearly been put together with a fair amount of thought. It's not as though the plot lacks interesting elements, the overall production quality is relatively high, and it generally knows how to hit the important beats. It also shows some promise for future developments, so I'm giving it a reasonably favorable score.

But seriously, whenever the members of the hero's party appear in those flashbacks, all I can think is, "Who the hell are these people?"

And I honestly can't make much sense of how their relationships have changed.

I'm guessing Romelia's difficult personality gradually caused her to get the short end of the stick, until both her fiancé and the other party members started finding her increasingly annoying. And then that blonde woman swooped in and stole her man—some kind of NTR situation, perhaps?

Is that what we're supposed to take away from it?

Because, man... the storytelling is sloppy.]

enjoymentRanking.comment_en:
Episode #7: The Message
"I love the atmosphere and the worldbuilding, but no matter how this arc develops, I just can't shake the feeling that the story still hasn't really begun."

[Under normal circumstances, this would probably have been an episode I'd give at least an 8, possibly even something in the 9s, with a chance of ranking among my favorites of the week. At least, that's the kind of quality—or perhaps the kind of story—it seemed to have.

But there's one problem that's been following this series around from the beginning, and I felt it particularly strongly again this time: I don't really understand the story, the characters, or even the world they inhabit. And precisely because everything is so mysterious and unfamiliar, I find it difficult to relate to the characters or become emotionally invested in what's happening. At least, that's how it feels to me personally.

In particular, I just can't bring myself to care much about this "Sleepless" guy or Eleonora.

Their awkwardness and embarrassment around each other? Sure, I can understand what's going on from what I'm shown, and at first I was even getting into it. But since I still barely know who these two people really are, my reaction gradually shifted to "...So what?" Eventually, I just stopped caring.

The same goes for everything else in this episode. There's whatever political or social situation is unfolding in the kingdom they're visiting—or is it even a kingdom? Then there's that incredibly powerful, godlike, handsome guy who's been running wild and apparently threatening the fairies behind the scenes to make them do his bidding, not to mention the flower fairy and all the other intriguing elements.

It's all interesting in principle, but none of it really sinks in. I can't get a proper grasp of what's going on, so I don't know what to make of any of it.

When Eleonora transforms from a bashful young woman into someone determined to stand up and protect Yoru—or the Sleepless guy, whatever his name is—and starts showing what seems to be her true character, it's undeniably cool. But that's about as far as my reaction goes. I appreciate it on a surface level without feeling much of anything deeper.

Whatever happens afterward, I find myself thinking, "Well, it's not like anyone's actually going to die..." And that's pretty much it.

I've liked the atmosphere and worldbuilding ever since the first episode, and I've enjoyed the series to a reasonable extent along the way. But even now, I still haven't escaped that feeling of "When is this story actually going to start?"

I just haven't managed to get into it, and I think that's what makes watching it so frustrating.]

Deep within the forest, a cozy and rather cluttered cottage sits on the lakeshore, housing a mysterious, feared witch. In truth, she is a lovely young woman named Rose, who has learned the art of potion-making from her wise grandmother. Rose cherishes her tucked-away life, yet there is a longing in her heart—for a handsome knight she once saw, Sir Harij Azm.
